# Major depressive disorder

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Obstetrics/gynecology > Puerperium > Major depressive disorder*

[Original Article Link](/library/PP0WUT)

---

## Summary

Major <u>depressive disorder</u> (MDD) is an episodic <u>mood disorder</u> primarily characterized by <u>depressed mood</u> and <u>anhedonia</u> lasting for at least two weeks. Women have a higher risk of developing MDD than men. The peak age of onset is the third decade. The etiology is multifactorial, including both biological and psychological factors. Reduced levels of <u>neurotransmitters</u> (<u>serotonin</u>, <u>noradrenaline</u>, <u>dopamine</u>) are believed to be the pathophysiological basis in most cases. Other <u>symptoms of MDD</u> include <u>sleep</u> disturbance, loss of appetite, and <u>thoughts of suicide</u>. <u>Subtypes of MDD</u> are characterized by additional symptoms. <u>MDD with atypical features</u> is additionally characterized by weight gain and increased appetite, while <u>MDD with psychotic features</u> is characterized by <u>hallucinations</u> and <u>delusions</u>. Presentations may also vary in special patient groups, e.g., pregnant patients, older patients, children and <u>adolescents</u>, and patients receiving <u>palliative care</u>. Treatment of all forms of MDD is multifaceted and often requires <u>psychotherapy</u>, pharmacotherapy (most commonly <u>SSRIs</u>), and lifestyle changes.

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Depressed mood</u>

* <u>Anhedonia</u>

* Feelings of guilt, worthlessness, or hopelessness

* Low energy levels

* Difficulty concentrating

* Changes in appetite and weight (increased or decreased)

* <u>Sleep disorders</u> (<u>insomnia</u> or <u>hypersomnia</u>)

* <u>Psychomotor agitation</u> or retardation

* <u>Suicidal thoughts</u>

* May additionally manifest with:

* Somatic features, e.g., <u>headaches</u>, <u>myalgia</u>, gastrointestinal problems

* Aggression, <u>substance use disorder</u>, or increase in risk-taking behavior





> [!TIP]
> <u>Older adults with depression</u> may be more likely than younger adults to present with physical symptoms than a low mood. [[6]](/library/X3c9SX0)




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Depression screening</u> with “<u>SIGECAPS</u>”: Sleep (<u>insomnia</u> or <u>hypersomnia</u>), Interest loss (<u>anhedonia</u>), Guilt (low self-esteem), Energy (low energy or fatigue), Concentration (poor concentration or difficulty making decisions), Appetite (decreased appetite or overeating), Psychomotor <u>agitation</u> or retardation, and Suicidality.




![Symptom-duration criteria for the diagnosis of mood disorders](media/zdenxblaj0g34nxaup30s6m1.jpg)

Symptom-duration criteria for the diagnosis of mood disorders

## Subtypes and variants

### Major depressive disorder with seasonal pattern (<u>seasonal affective disorder</u>, <u>winter depression</u>)




* Definition: a subtype of major <u>depressive disorder</u> characterized by ≥ 2 depressive episodes associated with a seasonal pattern (e.g., the winter season) over ≥ 2 years

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: occurs in a yearly, season-specific pattern (commonly in fall or winter)

* Clinical features

* Patients present with typical <u>symptoms of MDD</u> alongside atypical ones, such as weight gain and requiring more <u>sleep</u>.

* See “<u>Major depressive episode</u>” for details.

* Diagnostic criteria: Symptoms must be present for ≥ 2 consecutive years and for the majority of years in a lifetime.

* Treatment: <u>Bright light therapy</u> has been shown to improve symptoms.





### Major depressive disorder with atypical features




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: most common variant of MDD

* Clinical features

* Increased appetite or over-eating

* <u>Hypersomnia</u>

* Leaden <u>paralysis</u> (legs and arms feel heavy)

* <u>Interpersonal rejection sensitivity</u> that leads to social and occupational impairment

* Mood reactivity: brightening of mood in response to positive events, which is usually not the case in classical MDD

* Diagnostic criteria: two or more of the clinical features are present

* Treatment

* 1<sup>st</sup> line: <u>CBT</u> with or without <u>SSRIs</u>

* <u>MAO inhibitors</u> can be effective although not commonly prescribed due to their side effects.





### Major depressive disorder with psychotic features




* Definition: major <u>depression</u> accompanied by <u>psychotic symptoms</u>

* Etiology: overactivity of the <u>hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis</u> (increased <u>dopamine</u> activity) is believed to play a major role.

* Clinical features: See “<u>Major depressive episode</u>” and “<u>Psychotic features</u>” for details.

* Diagnostic criteria

* <u>Features of MDD</u> (see <u>diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder</u>)

* <u>Psychotic features</u>, such as <u>delusions</u> and <u>hallucinations</u>, which are usually <u>mood-congruent</u> (<u>delusions</u> and <u>hallucinations</u> are often about worthlessness, guilt, <u>death</u>, and hopelessness)

* <u>Psychotic features</u> occur only alongside a <u>major depressive episode</u>.

* Treatment

* <u>Antidepressants</u> together with <u>atypical antipsychotics</u>

* In severe cases, <u>electroconvulsive therapy</u> may be used.





References:[[7]](/library/QtauWm)[[8]](/library/Nta-dm)

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[9]](/library/1rc2Td0)




* Screen all adults using a brief screening tool, e.g., <u>Patient Health Questionnaire-2</u>.

* If screening is positive, perform a full clinical assessment, including:

* Confirmation of diagnosis using <u>DSM-5 criteria for MDD</u>

* Determination of severity: Combined tools for screening and severity assessment can be used, e.g., <u>Patient Health Questionnaire-9</u>.

* Assessment of <u>suicide</u> risk

* Diagnostic studies for common differential diagnoses

* Identification of psychiatric and medical comorbidities





### Screening for depression [[5]](/library/MScMZX0)[[10]](/library/7PW4Tl0)




#### Overview




* Screen all adults aged ≥ 18 years and children aged ≥ 12 years.

* Recommended screening intervals [[5]](/library/MScMZX0)

* Adults: Optimum intervals are unclear; screen at least once and consider repeating either when <u>risk factors</u> arise or at routine health checks.

* Children aged ≥ 12 years: Screen annually until 18–21 years of age.  [[11]](/library/JN1sXh0)





#### Brief screening tool




* Use the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (<u>PHQ-2</u>).

* A 2-item survey for assessing <u>depressed mood</u> and loss of interest or pleasure in activities over the last 2 weeks

* A score ≥ 3 is considered positive; follow up with a full clinical assessment.





![Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2)](media/xf61co00khqhbkipuryo7bjj.jpg)

Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2)




#### Further screening tools




* Scores that also assess severity:

* Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (<u>PHQ-9</u>)  [[12]](/library/9AcNNU0)

* Major depression inventory

* Beck Depression Inventory (<u>BDI</u>)  [[13]](/library/1n12Hh0)

* Consider using specific screening scores  when assessing for <u>depression in special patient groups</u>. [[10]](/library/7PW4Tl0)





![Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9)](media/psjj9hai8u91kao526t96kam.jpg)

Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9)

![Major Depression Inventory](media/pr6a8otsqoho3tnwuj0vkrny.jpg)

Major Depression Inventory




### Diagnostic criteria




| <br>Diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder(consistent with <u>DSM-5</u>) [[8]](/library/Nta-dm)[[14]](/library/Vn1GHh0)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| A | <br>Five or more of the nine symptoms listed below, for at least 2 weeks, with at least one of the symptoms being <u>depressed mood</u> or <u>anhedonia</u> <br>1. * <u>Depressed mood</u> for most of the day, almost every day (in children, can manifest with irritability)<br>2. * <u>Sleep</u> disturbance (<u>insomnia</u> or <u>hypersomnia</u>)<br>3. * <u>Anhedonia</u><br>4. * Feelings of worthlessness or disproportionate guilt<br>5. * Fatigue or loss of energy<br>6. * Diminished concentration, <u>cognition</u>, and ability to make decisions (<u>pseudodementia</u>)<br>7. * Weight change due to appetite change<br>8. * Psychomotor changes (observed by others)<br><br>* <u>Agitation</u><br><br>* Retardation<br>9. * <u>Suicidal ideation</u><br><br><br> |
| B | There is clinically significant <u>distress</u> or impaired functioning in important areas of life (e.g., work, school). |
| C | Symptoms are not due to the effects of psychoactive substances or organic disease. |
| D | <br>Symptoms are not superimposed upon or due to <u>schizoaffective disorder</u> or another <u>psychotic disorder</u>. <br> |
| E | There is no history of a <u>manic</u> or <u>hypomanic episode</u>. |
| <br><br>* Criteria A-C are met: major depressive episode<br><br>* Criteria A-E are met: major depressive disorder<br><br><br> |  |





#### Severity (according to <u>DSM-5</u>) [[8]](/library/Nta-dm)




Treatment recommendations are often categorized by severity:




* Mild: minimal number of symptoms to fulfill diagnostic requirements PLUS manageable symptom intensity PLUS minor impaired functioning

* Moderate: number of symptoms, symptom intensity, and impaired functioning greater than “mild” but less than “severe”

* Severe: number of symptoms more than fulfill diagnostic requirements PLUS unmanageable symptom intensity PLUS extremely impaired functioning





> [!TIP]
> Depressive episodes are considered recurrent when there is a gap of at least two months between episodes during which the criteria for MDD are not met.




### Further assessment [[5]](/library/MScMZX0)




#### <u>Suicide</u> risk [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)[[16]](/library/0xceEe0)




* Screen all patients with MDD for <u>suicidality</u>. [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)[[16]](/library/0xceEe0)

* Screening tools include the <u>Ask Suicide-Screening Questions suicide risk screening tool</u> and the <u>Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale</u>.

* A comprehensive assessment includes consideration of <u>risk factors for suicide</u> and protective factors.

* See also “<u>Suicide risk evaluation</u>.”





![Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale](media/x76cdcnommxa7ungijklpekw.jpg)

Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale




#### Exclusion of organic causes of depression [[5]](/library/MScMZX0)[[15]](/library/oSc00X0)




* Comprehensive history and <u>physical examination</u>

* Assess patients for features of physical diseases that mimic <u>depression</u>, e.g., <u>clinical features of hypothyroidism</u>.

* Screen for drugs associated with <u>medication-induced depressive disorder</u>, e.g., <u>beta blockers</u>, <u>glucocorticoids</u>, <u>oral contraceptives</u>.

* <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[5]](/library/MScMZX0)[[15]](/library/oSc00X0)

* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>

* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>CMP</u>

* <u>Vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u>

* <u>Folate</u>

* Consider the following based on clinical suspicion:

* Serum and urine toxicology  [[17]](/library/X_c95U0)[[18]](/library/1_c2MU0)

* <u>HIV testing</u>

* <u>Syphilis screening</u>

* <u>Diagnostic studies for Lyme disease</u>

* <u>Testosterone</u> levels (<u>♂</u>)

* <u>Neuroimaging</u>: Consider evaluating for structural <u>brain</u> disease based on clinical presentation. [[19]](/library/W3cPhX0)

* <u>Cognitive testing</u>: to assess for <u>memory</u> issues and <u>dementia</u> [[6]](/library/X3c9SX0)

* <u>Polysomnography</u> (<u>PSG</u>): not routinely performed but obtained if a concurrent primary <u>sleep disorder</u> is suspected  [[20]](/library/6r1jRR0)

* <u>Sleep</u> disturbances are associated with various psychiatric conditions, but most commonly occur in <u>mood disorders</u>.

* Results obtained during <u>PSG</u> can be helpful in differentiating mood-disorder-associated <u>sleep</u> abnormalities from primary <u>sleep disorders</u>.

* <u>PSG</u> findings in <u>depression</u> include:

* <u>REM sleep</u> abnormalities

* ↓ <u>REM latency</u>: associated with a number of depressive symptoms, including early morning awakening and <u>anhedonia</u>

* ↑ <u>REM</u> activity and density

* <u>Sleep</u> continuity disturbances

* Reduced <u>slow-wave sleep</u>





![Comparison of sleep phases in healthy and depressed individuals](media/g43gxg1o85m8dk0bh13ryuur.jpg)

Comparison of sleep phases in healthy and depressed individuals




#### Consideration of alternative diagnoses [[5]](/library/MScMZX0)[[15]](/library/oSc00X0)




* <u>Bipolar disorder</u>

* BD should be considered in patients with <u>treatment-resistant depression</u> or unexpected responses to <u>antidepressants</u> (e.g., <u>manic</u> or <u>hypomanic</u> symptoms)

* Screening tools include:

* Mood disorder questionnaire (<u>MDQ</u>): self-report instrument used to assess and monitor for symptoms of <u>bipolar disorder</u> and other <u>mood disorders</u> 

* Completion takes approx. 5 minutes.

* Consists of 13 yes-or-no questions

* Items include having more energy than usual and being more talkative or speaking more quickly than usual.

* Most sensitive for <u>bipolar I disorder</u> [[21]](/library/sG1t0i0)

* Reported <u>sensitivity</u> is 0.28–0.73 and <u>specificity</u> is 0.67–0.97. [[22]](/library/FG1gai0)

* Hypomania checklist (<u>HCL-32</u>): a self-report instrument used to identify <u>hypomanic</u> symptoms in the diagnosis of <u>bipolar disorder</u>; mostly used in patients with <u>depression</u>.

* Consists of 32 yes-or-no questions

* A score of > 13 is considered positive for <u>hypomania</u>.

* Reported overall <u>sensitivity</u> is 80% with a <u>specificity</u> of 65% in patients with a <u>mood disorder</u>. [[23]](/library/EG18ai0)

* Early diagnosis and treatment of BD is vital due to the high frequency of self-harm, <u>suicide</u>, and other complications associated with the condition.

* Studies report misdiagnosis rates for BD of up to 80%. [[24]](/library/9u1Nti0)

* Reported estimates of unrecognized <u>bipolar disorder</u> in patients treated for <u>depression</u> range from 10–20%. [[21]](/library/sG1t0i0)[[25]](/library/GG1B0i0)

* <u>Schizophrenia</u>: <u>Negative symptoms of schizophrenia</u> may be mistaken for <u>depression</u>.

* Other <u>depressive disorders</u>: e.g., <u>adjustment disorder</u> or <u>persistent depressive disorder</u> (see “Differential diagnoses of MDD”)  [[26]](/library/qBcCbU0)





> [!TIP]
> Assess all patients presenting with <u>depression</u> for past episodes of <u>mania</u> and/or <u>hypomania</u> to rule out <u>bipolar disorder</u>. Patients with <u>bipolar disorder</u> who are treated with <u>antidepressants</u> without a <u>mood stabilizer</u> are at increased risk of <u>manic symptoms</u>. [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)




![Mood Disorder Questionnaire](media/ttxibauvsyeyqp03zod3ydio.jpg)

Mood Disorder Questionnaire




#### Identification of potential psychiatric comorbidities




* <u>Anxiety</u>: most common comorbidity; screen using the <u>GAD-7 scale</u>.   [[12]](/library/9AcNNU0)[[15]](/library/oSc00X0)[[27]](/library/IBcYXU0)[[28]](/library/A_cRIU0)

* <u>Alcohol</u> and <u>substance use disorder</u>

* <u>Personality disorders</u>

* <u>ADHD</u>  [[29]](/library/JBcsbU0)





![GAD-7 anxiety scale](media/jnmizxrh8blu41o87b9zd603.jpg)

GAD-7 anxiety scale

## Treatment

The treatment advice in this section applies to the general adult population. For <u>depression</u> in other patient groups (e.g., older adults, children, patients with cancer), see “<u>Depression in special patient groups</u>.”




### Approach [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)[[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[31]](/library/4GY3zq)




* Advise patients on lifestyle modifications.  [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)

* Start initial treatment based on severity.

* Mild <u>depression</u>: typically <u>psychotherapy</u> alone [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)[[32]](/library/H41KkS0)

* Moderate and severe <u>depression</u>: <u>psychotherapy</u> and pharmacotherapy  [[31]](/library/4GY3zq)[[32]](/library/H41KkS0)[[33]](/library/s41tkS0)

* Urgently refer patients with severe/complex <u>depression</u> or <u>suicidality</u> to <u>psychiatry</u>; admission may be required.

* Provide the patient and their family with information on <u>depression</u> (see “<u>Managing chronic conditions</u>”).

* Ensure patients receive treatment for:

* Psychiatric comorbidities, e.g., <u>alcohol use disorder</u>

* Contributing physical conditions  [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)

* Review patients regularly; assess the <u>efficacy</u> of treatment at ∼ 6 weeks and consider modifications.  [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)





### Lifestyle modifications   [[34]](/library/b41H3S0)




* <u>Sleep hygiene</u>  [[35]](/library/P41WjS0)[[36]](/library/j41_QS0)

* Reduction in substance use, e.g., <u>alcohol</u>, <u>recreational drugs</u>  [[37]](/library/Q41uQS0)

* <u>Stress</u> reduction

* Increasing social support

* Regular aerobic exercise [[38]](/library/h41cQS0)[[39]](/library/341SQS0)

* Relaxation/<u>mindfulness</u> [[40]](/library/R41lQS0)

* Improved nutrition   [[34]](/library/b41H3S0)[[41]](/library/S41yiS0)





> [!TIP]
> Lifestyle modifications are more effective when individualized to the patient.




### <u>Psychotherapy</u> [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)[[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[31]](/library/4GY3zq)




* May be used alone or in combination with pharmacotherapy

* Options include:

* <u>Cognitive behavioral therapy</u> (<u>CBT</u>)

* <u>Interpersonal therapy</u>

* <u>Behavioral activation</u>

* <u>Psychodynamic psychotherapy</u>

* <u>Supportive psychotherapy</u>





> [!TIP]
> There is no evidence to support the use of one modality of <u>psychotherapy</u> over another for the <u>treatment of MDD</u>. [[31]](/library/4GY3zq)




### Initial pharmacotherapy [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)[[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[31]](/library/4GY3zq)




#### Initiation




* Choice of initial medication

* Most <u>antidepressants</u> have comparable <u>efficacy</u> but different adverse effects.

* When choosing an <u>antidepressant</u>, consider:

* Psychiatric and medical comorbidities

* Current symptoms

* Previous treatment experiences

* Medication adverse effects

* Interactions with other medications

* Initial medication trial

* Typically requires ≥ 4 weeks to take effect

* Start with the lowest dose and increase slowly (e.g., with dose adjustments every 2 weeks).

* Monitor for <u>suicidal ideation</u>, <u>manic symptoms</u>, <u>psychotic symptoms</u>, and <u>agitation</u>. [[42]](/library/dhco1X0)





#### First-line antidepressant medications




* Options include <u>SSRIs</u> (often trialed first), <u>SNRIs</u>, and the <u>atypical antidepressants</u> <u>bupropion</u> and <u>mirtazapine</u>.

* For further information on adverse effects and contraindications, see “<u>Antidepressants</u>.”





| <br>First-line medications for the <u>treatment of major depressive disorder</u> [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)[[30]](/library/bWXHPC)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Drug class |  | Examples | Important considerations |
| <u>SSRIs</u> |  | <br><br>* <u>Fluoxetine</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Paroxetine</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Sertraline</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Citalopram</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Escitalopram</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Associated with sexual adverse effects<br><br>* <u>Escitalopram</u> may have fewer general adverse effects than other <u>SSRIs</u> and <u>SNRIs</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <u>SNRIs</u> |  | <br><br>* <u>Venlafaxine</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Desvenlafaxine</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Duloxetine</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Duloxetine</u> may be preferable for patients with concomitant neuropathic and <u>chronic pain</u>.<br><br> |
| <u>Atypical antidepressants</u> |  | <br>* <u>Bupropion</u> DOSAGE<br><br> | <br><br>* Reduced <u>sexual dysfunction</u> compared to <u>SSRIs</u><br><br>* Can also be used for <u>smoking cessation</u><br><br>* May increase <u>anxiety</u> and lower <u>seizure</u> threshold<br><br><br> |
| <br>* <u>Mirtazapine</u> DOSAGE<br><br> | <br>* Can cause sedation and weight gain, which may be desirable for some patients (e.g., those with <u>insomnia</u> or poor appetite)<br><br> |  |  |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>SSRIs</u> and <u>venlafaxine</u> have been associated with an increased risk of <u>suicidality</u> in adults aged < 24 years. Monitor patients starting <u>antidepressants</u> carefully for side effects and worsening of depressive symptoms. [[43]](/library/Rk1lnS0)




#### Other <u>antidepressant</u> medications




* These medications cause more adverse effects than first-line therapies (e.g., <u>SSRIs</u>). [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)

* Options include:

* <u>Trazodone</u>: used primarily for <u>insomnia</u>; a higher dose is required when used as an <u>antidepressant</u> [[44]](/library/aWXQPC)

* <u>Tricyclic antidepressants</u>, e.g., <u>amitriptyline</u>, <u>nortriptyline</u>

* <u>Monoamine oxidase inhibitors</u> (<u>MAOIs</u>), e.g., <u>phenelzine</u>





> [!WARNING]
> <u>MAOIs</u> should not be combined with <u>SSRIs</u>/<u>SNRIs</u> or <u>tricyclic antidepressants</u>, because this may lead to <u>serotonin syndrome</u>. [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)




### Ongoing management




#### Monitoring treatment <u>efficacy</u>




* Monitor treatment response using an objective score of symptom severity, e.g., <u>PHQ-9</u>. [[45]](/library/UAcbQU0)

* Determine next steps after ∼ 6 weeks of good adherence to treatment. [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)





| <br>Ongoing <u>management of depression</u> [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)[[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[31]](/library/4GY3zq)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treatment response |  | Recommended actions |
| Minimal or no response |  | <br>* Depending on the initial treatment modality, consider:<br><br>* Starting or changing first-line <u>antidepressants</u><br><br>* Starting or changing <u>psychotherapy</u><br><br> |
| Partial response |  | <br><br>* For patients receiving <u>psychotherapy</u> alone, consider:<br><br>* Addition of an <u>antidepressant</u><br><br>* Change of <u>psychotherapy</u><br><br>* For patients receiving <u>antidepressant</u> or combination therapy, consider:<br><br>* Addition or change of <u>psychotherapy</u><br><br>* Uptitrating the <u>antidepressant</u> dose as needed until the maximum dose is reached<br><br>* Use of <u>augmenting agents for depression</u><br><br><br> |
| Remission |  | <br><br>* Continue treatment; duration depends on the risk of relapse. [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)[[30]](/library/bWXHPC)<br><br>* Low risk: ≥ 6 months<br><br>* High risk : ≥ 2 years, or potentially lifelong<br><br>* Offer/continue <u>psychotherapy</u> for relapse prevention.<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> If an <u>antidepressant</u> has an insufficient effect, always assess the patient's <u>medication adherence</u> before adjusting the treatment plan. [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)




#### Switching or discontinuing <u>antidepressants</u> [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[31]](/library/4GY3zq)




* When switching between <u>antidepressants</u>, consider medication class and the risk of <u>serotonin syndrome</u>. [[46]](/library/Sk1yMS0)

* From one <u>SSRI</u> (excluding <u>fluoxetine</u>)  to another <u>SSRI</u> or <u>SNRI</u>: usually a direct switch  [[46]](/library/Sk1yMS0)[[47]](/library/7k146S0)

* To or from non-<u>MAOI</u> classes: usually <u>cross taper</u>  [[46]](/library/Sk1yMS0)

* To or from an <u>MAOI</u>: Taper completely, followed by a 2–6 week <u>washout period</u>.  [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)

* When discontinuing medications:

* Consider tapering over 6–8 weeks to : [[48]](/library/Dk11JS0)[[49]](/library/Ek18pS0)[[50]](/library/wk1hJS0)

* Decrease the risk of relapse

* Prevent <u>antidepressant discontinuation syndrome</u>

* Offer <u>psychotherapy</u> to prevent relapse.





> [!WARNING]
> When changing between <u>antidepressants</u>, monitor patients carefully for the development of <u>serotonin syndrome</u>. [[44]](/library/aWXQPC)




> [!NOTE]
> Symptoms of <u>antidepressant discontinuation syndrome</u> occur when treatment is FINISHed: Flu-like symptoms, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance, Sensory disturbances, Hyperarousal [[51]](/library/-hcDgX0)




### Treatment-resistant depression [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[52]](/library/Vk1G5S0)




* Definition: MDD that persists despite trials of ≥ 2 <u>antidepressants</u> at optimal doses [[52]](/library/Vk1G5S0)[[53]](/library/hk1cnS0)[[54]](/library/ek1x5S0)

* Should not be diagnosed without assessing patients for:

* Comorbid psychiatric conditions (e.g., <u>anxiety</u>, <u>substance use disorder</u>)

* Adherence to <u>antidepressant</u> therapy





#### Management




* Refer all patients to a <u>psychiatrist</u> to determine further treatment.

* Augmenting agents for depression [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[55]](/library/1xc2ve0)

* <u>Lithium</u>  [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[55]](/library/1xc2ve0)

* <u>Second-generation antipsychotics</u> (e.g., <u>aripiprazole</u>)

* <u>Thyroid hormones</u>

* <u>Ketamine</u>  [[52]](/library/Vk1G5S0)[[55]](/library/1xc2ve0)[[56]](/library/8HcOHd0)

* <u>Anticonvulsant</u> <u>mood stabilizers</u> (e.g., <u>lamotrigine</u>)

* Stimulants (e.g., <u>methylphenidate</u>)

* Neurostimulation therapy [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)

* <u>Electroconvulsive therapy</u> (<u>ECT</u>)

* Highly effective treatment for treatment-resistant MDD and severe MDD   [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[57]](/library/lk1vLS0)

* Accessibility and patient acceptance have limited its use.  [[52]](/library/Vk1G5S0)[[57]](/library/lk1vLS0)

* Requires regular attendance for intensive therapy followed by a gradual taper  [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[57]](/library/lk1vLS0)

* <u>Vagal nerve</u> stimulation

* <u>Transcranial magnetic stimulation</u>





> [!TIP]
> Consider <u>ECT</u> for patients with <u>treatment-resistant depression</u>, <u>depression</u> with <u>psychotic features</u>, <u>catatonia</u>, or a high risk of <u>suicide</u>. [[58]](/library/t_cXJU0)




### Additional therapies [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[31]](/library/4GY3zq)




The following therapies are not recommended as first-line, have variable evidence to support their use, and should be performed under specialist guidance.




* Complementary and alternative therapy [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[59]](/library/C41qlS0)

* Used by some patients as an alternative to <u>antidepressants</u> and/or <u>psychotherapy</u>

* Exercise monotherapy can be considered for mild <u>depression</u>.  [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[60]](/library/941NlS0)

* Herbal remedies, e.g., <u>St. John's wort</u>, are typically advised against because potential risks outweigh benefits.  [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[59]](/library/C41qlS0)

* Bright-light therapy: daily exposure to a <u>light intensity</u> of 5000–10,000 lux  [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[61]](/library/D411lS0)

* Used to treat <u>seasonal affective disorder</u> and may be used as an alternative or adjunctive treatment option in MDD

* Patients should be monitored for <u>hypomania</u>.

* Sleep deprivation therapy  [[62]](/library/w41hlS0)[[63]](/library/2RcTmX0)[[64]](/library/fRckmX0)

* A structured regimen of <u>sleep restriction</u> used alone or in conjunction with <u>bright-light therapy</u>

* Thought to cause a rapid but transient improvement in depressive symptoms  [[64]](/library/fRckmX0)

* Risk of inducing <u>mania</u> or <u>seizures</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Shared decision-making</u> should be used to plan treatment, taking into consideration previous experience of <u>MDD treatment</u>. [[31]](/library/4GY3zq)




> [!WARNING]
> Patients with <u>symptoms of psychosis</u> or <u>suicidal ideation</u> should be urgently referred to a <u>psychiatrist</u> or evaluated in the emergency department; if patients at risk of <u>suicide</u> are deemed safe for outpatient management they should be given details of a <u>suicide</u> crisis line as part of a comprehensive <u>suicide safety plan</u>. [[15]](/library/oSc00X0)[[27]](/library/IBcYXU0)

---

## Special patient groups

The diagnosis and treatment of <u>depression in special patient groups</u> is broadly the same as for the general adult population, with some modifications.




### Depression in children and adolescents [[31]](/library/4GY3zq)[[65]](/library/Yl1nvS0)[[66]](/library/al1QvS0)




#### Overview




* ∼ 15% of <u>adolescents</u> (12–17 years of age) report major <u>depression</u> in the past 12 months.  [[66]](/library/al1QvS0)[[67]](/library/bl1HvS0)

* The presentation of <u>depression in children</u> may differ from adults. [[11]](/library/JN1sXh0)[[31]](/library/4GY3zq)

* Classical <u>clinical features of MDD</u> may be less marked.

* Some symptoms may resemble those of <u>attention deficit hyperactivity disorder</u>, e.g.: [[68]](/library/d51oQh0)

* Irritability

* Difficulty concentrating or worsening performance at school

* Psychiatric comorbidities are common, e.g.: [[31]](/library/4GY3zq)

* <u>Conduct disorder</u> or <u>oppositional defiant disorder</u>

* <u>Anxiety</u>

* <u>Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder</u>





#### Diagnosis [[66]](/library/al1QvS0)




* See “<u>Diagnosis of MDD</u>.”

* Consider using the <u>PHQ-9 modified for adolescents</u> to <u>screen for depression</u>.

* <u>Diagnostic criteria for MDD</u> are the same as for adults, with two exceptions: [[8]](/library/Nta-dm)

* Irritability can be noted in the assessment of mood.

* Failure to gain weight can be noted in the assessment of appetite.





#### Treatment of depression in children [[11]](/library/JN1sXh0)[[65]](/library/Yl1nvS0)[[66]](/library/al1QvS0)




* Mild <u>depression</u>: Consider 6–8 weeks of active support and monitoring.  [[65]](/library/Yl1nvS0)

* Moderate to severe <u>depression</u> or refractory mild <u>depression</u>

* Initiate <u>treatment of MDD</u> with <u>psychotherapy</u> and/or pharmacotherapy. [[65]](/library/Yl1nvS0)

* For <u>psychotherapy</u>, <u>CBT</u> and <u>interpersonal therapy for adolescents</u> are preferred.

* Patients requiring pharmacotherapy

* First-line: <u>SSRIs</u>  [[66]](/library/al1QvS0)

* Monitor for adverse effects, including <u>suicidality</u>.  [[65]](/library/Yl1nvS0)

* Continue treatment and monitoring for 6–12 months after the resolution of symptoms. [[65]](/library/Yl1nvS0)





> [!WARNING]
> Monitor all children starting on <u>SSRIs</u> for <u>suicidality</u>. [[65]](/library/Yl1nvS0)




### Depression in older adults [[6]](/library/X3c9SX0)[[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[31]](/library/4GY3zq)




#### Overview




* <u>MDD in older adults</u> (<u>late-life depression</u>) is common.  [[69]](/library/yAcdmU0)

* <u>Risk factors</u> include: [[5]](/library/MScMZX0)

* Social isolation

* <u>Death</u> of a spouse

* Low <u>socioeconomic status</u>

* Comorbid physical illness including uncontrolled <u>pain</u>

* Impairments to <u>cognition</u> and functioning

* Older patients may present atypically with irritability, <u>anxiety</u>, or physical symptoms as opposed to low mood. [[6]](/library/X3c9SX0)





#### Diagnosis




* See “<u>Diagnosis of MDD</u>.”

* Consider using an adapted screening score, e.g., the Geriatric Depression Scale-15.

* Neurological disease and coexisting medical conditions are more common in this patient group; work up thoroughly to exclude physical causes.

* Older adults have an elevated <u>suicide</u> risk; screen carefully for <u>suicidality</u>. [[5]](/library/MScMZX0)





![Geriatric Depression Scale-15](media/jwmz0xr35f6vqwjp6czrcznu.jpg)

Geriatric Depression Scale-15




#### Treatment




* Lifestyle changes: Exercise may be particularly beneficial. [[6]](/library/X3c9SX0)

* Pharmacotherapy: Older adults have an increased risk of adverse effects from medications (see “<u>Pharmacology for older adults</u>”). [[6]](/library/X3c9SX0)[[70]](/library/BPdzSJ0)

* <u>SSRIs</u>: preferred first-line treatment in individuals aged ≥ 60 years  [[6]](/library/X3c9SX0)

* Consider using reduced frequencies and/or lower doses than in the general adult population.

* Minimize <u>polypharmacy</u> whenever possible.

* <u>Psychotherapy</u>: Consider modifications in patients with cognitive impairment; <u>problem-solving therapy</u> may be effective. [[6]](/library/X3c9SX0)

* <u>ECT</u>: highly effective; response rates are higher in adults aged > 65 years than in younger adults. [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)

* See “<u>Treatment of MDD</u>” for details.





> [!TIP]
> Cognitive impairment should be considered as a possible underlying cause of <u>depression in older adults</u>. [[6]](/library/X3c9SX0)




> [!WARNING]
> In older patients, monitor for <u>hyponatremia</u> after starting or adjusting the dosages of <u>SSRIs</u>, <u>SNRIs</u>, <u>TCAs</u>, or <u>mirtazapine</u>. [[70]](/library/BPdzSJ0)




### Depression in patients receiving palliative care [[71]](/library/W51PQh0)




#### Overview




* Depressive symptoms or <u>thoughts of suicide</u> are common in patients with a limited <u>life expectancy</u>.  [[71]](/library/W51PQh0)[[72]](/library/cl1aDS0)

* <u>Symptoms of depression</u> (e.g., changes in appetite, low energy, impaired <u>sleep</u>) may overlap with : [[71]](/library/W51PQh0)[[73]](/library/651jOh0)[[74]](/library/Xl19vS0)

* Symptoms of an underlying medical condition

* Adverse effects of treatment

* <u>Grief</u>





#### Diagnosis [[75]](/library/1l12DS0)




* See “<u>Diagnosis of MDD</u>.”

* <u>Screen for depression</u> at diagnosis of a life-limiting illness and periodically thereafter. [[75]](/library/1l12DS0)

* Identify physical symptoms that may contribute to low mood (see “<u>Principles of cancer care</u>”).





#### Treatment [[71]](/library/W51PQh0)[[73]](/library/651jOh0)




* <u>Psychotherapy</u> is first-line treatment for mild to moderate <u>depression</u>.

* The choice of <u>antidepressant</u> is based on symptoms and comorbidities.

* <u>SSRIs</u> are typically used first-line because they have the lowest risk of adverse effects and interactions. [[73]](/library/651jOh0)[[76]](/library/HbcKEa0)

* <u>Antidepressants</u> may be selected because they have a dual function. [[73]](/library/651jOh0)

* Consider a tricyclic or <u>SNRI</u> if the patient also has <u>neuropathic pain</u>.

* Use <u>mirtazapine</u> if patients have poor appetite or <u>insomnia</u>.

* <u>Psychostimulants</u> (e.g., <u>methylphenidate</u>) are sometimes used for patients with limited <u>life expectancy</u>.  [[71]](/library/W51PQh0)[[77]](/library/p51LOh0)

* See “<u>Treatment of MDD</u>” for details.





> [!TIP]
> Consider <u>life expectancy</u> when selecting <u>treatment for depression</u> in patients near the end of life; many <u>antidepressants</u> can take several weeks to have an effect. [[71]](/library/W51PQh0)




### Depression in patients with cancer [[73]](/library/651jOh0)[[75]](/library/1l12DS0)




MDD is more common in patients with cancer than in the general population.  [[78]](/library/mI1VWR0)




#### Diagnosis




* See “<u>Diagnosis of MDD</u>.”

* Clinical clues may include: [[75]](/library/1l12DS0)

* <u>Poor adherence</u> to treatment regimens

* Difficulty with referral follow-through

* <u>Anhedonia</u> that goes beyond the expected reaction of receiving a cancer diagnosis

* Screening [[75]](/library/1l12DS0)

* Actively <u>screen for depression</u> at time of original cancer diagnosis, regularly throughout cancer therapy, and when significant life events occur, e.g., in the case of cancer progression or recurrence, changes in therapy, entering into <u>palliative care</u>, or personal/social <u>distress</u>.

* The American Society of Clinical Oncology recommends the <u>PHQ-2</u> and <u>PHQ-9</u> screening tools for initial assessment.

* Assessment of MDD in patients with cancer can be complicated due to overlapping somatic symptoms like fatigue, <u>insomnia</u> or <u>hypersomnia</u>, weight loss, and cognitive impairment. [[79]](/library/lI1v1R0)

* <u>Insomnia</u> or <u>hypersomnia</u> can be caused by poorly controlled <u>pain</u> or <u>CNS</u> <u>malignancy</u>.

* Fatigue can be due to <u>malignancy</u>, radiation, <u>chemotherapy</u>, or <u>anemia</u> (see <u>cancer-related fatigue</u>).

* Weight loss can be caused by <u>cancer anorexia-cachexia syndrome</u>, <u>chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting</u>, or <u>chemotherapy-induced diarrhea</u>.

* Cognitive impairment can be caused by <u>CNS</u> <u>malignancy</u>, <u>chemotherapy</u>, <u>hormone</u> therapy, or radiation.





#### Treatment [[73]](/library/651jOh0)[[79]](/library/lI1v1R0)




* Treat cancer <u>pain</u> and other physical symptoms.  [[79]](/library/lI1v1R0)

* The choice of <u>antidepressants</u> is based on symptoms and comorbidities. [[73]](/library/651jOh0)

* <u>SSRIs</u> are typically used first-line because they have the lowest risk of adverse effects and interactions.

* Many <u>antidepressants</u> have a dual function that may benefit patients, e.g.:

* Consider a tricyclic or <u>SNRI</u> if the patient also has <u>neuropathic pain</u>.

* Use <u>mirtazapine</u> if the patient has poor appetite, <u>nausea</u>, or <u>insomnia</u>.

* See “<u>Treatment of MDD</u>” for details.





### Depression post myocardial infarction [[80]](/library/Yr1nfR0)




#### Overview




* The risk of <u>depression</u> in individuals post <u>MI</u> is approx. three times that of the general population.  [[81]](/library/8r1OQR0)

* <u>Depression post MI</u> is associated with an increased risk of further adverse cardiovascular events.





#### Diagnosis




* See “<u>Diagnosis of MDD</u>.”

* Screening

* All patients with cardiovascular disease should be screened for <u>depression</u>.

* The American <u>Heart</u> Association recommends the <u>PHQ-2</u> and <u>PHQ-9</u> screening tools for initial assessment.





#### Treatment




* First-line treatment includes <u>SSRIs</u>, <u>psychotherapy</u>, and/or moderate exercise.

* <u>SNRIs</u> may increase the risk of <u>hypertension</u> and <u>tachycardia</u>.

* Avoid tricyclics due to their cardiotoxic effects.

* See “<u>Treatment of MDD</u>” for details.

---

## Depression in the peripartum period

### Peripartum depression




MDD that occurs during <u>pregnancy</u> or after delivery  [[8]](/library/Nta-dm)[[82]](/library/sO1tFS0)[[83]](/library/AO1RES0)




#### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* Affects up to 14% of <u>pregnancies</u> [[84]](/library/wN1hWh0)

* Risk factors for peripartum depression include: [[82]](/library/sO1tFS0)[[85]](/library/1MW2nN0)

* Personal or <u>family history</u> of <u>depression</u>

* History of <u>intimate partner violence</u>

* Unplanned or <u>undesired pregnancy</u>

* Medical complications during <u>pregnancy</u>

* Poor support network

* Financial <u>stress</u>

* Patients with a previous history of <u>depression</u> are at increased risk of developing <u>peripartum depression</u>.





#### Diagnostics of peripartum depression




* See “<u>Diagnosis of MDD</u>.”

* Screening [[10]](/library/7PW4Tl0)[[86]](/library/HO1KFS0)[[87]](/library/uO1p8S0)

* Screen at least once in the peripartum period.  [[10]](/library/7PW4Tl0)[[88]](/library/7O14FS0)[[89]](/library/aPWQWl0)

* Consider using a modified screening tool, e.g., the Edinburgh <u>postnatal depression</u> scale.

* For patients with a positive screen: [[89]](/library/aPWQWl0)

* Screen for <u>bipolar disorder</u>, e.g., using the <u>MDQ</u>.

* Screen for infanticidal thoughts as well as <u>suicidality</u>. [[82]](/library/sO1tFS0)[[90]](/library/Hm1KSh0)





![Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale](media/f6162zxq5dtpturxl750cyst.jpg)

Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale




#### Treatment of peripartum depression




<u>Treatment of peripartum depression</u> is broadly the same as for the general adult population (see “<u>Treatment of MDD</u>”), with some modifications.




##### Antenatal considerations




* Offer <u>psychotherapy</u> as an alternative to pharmacotherapy in mild to moderate <u>depression</u>.

* Discontinuation of pharmacotherapy can be considered in stable patients with a known <u>diagnosis of MDD</u>.  [[91]](/library/zO1rES0)

* Patients starting or continuing <u>antidepressants</u>: Educate on the risks and benefits of <u>antidepressants</u> and monitor carefully.  [[91]](/library/zO1rES0)

* Avoid <u>paroxetine</u> during <u>pregnancy</u> because of the potential risk of cardiac anomalies. [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)

* Use monotherapy whenever possible.





##### Postpartum considerations




* Patients already on <u>SSRIs</u>, <u>SNRIs</u>, <u>TCAs</u>, and <u>mirtazapine</u> can continue treatment while <u>breastfeeding</u>. [[92]](/library/Q51uPh0)

* In patients starting <u>antidepressants</u>, begin with a medication that has few side effects and minimal transfer to <u>breastmilk</u>, e.g., <u>sertraline</u>.  [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)[[82]](/library/sO1tFS0)[[92]](/library/Q51uPh0)

* Newer alternatives include :

* <u>Brexanolone</u> infusion  [[93]](/library/xgWExk0)

* <u>Zuranolone</u> DOSAGE [[94]](/library/lLWvBN0)

* Mother and baby units are preferred for patients requiring hospitalization. [[95]](/library/9m1N3h0)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Depression</u> has adverse effects on maternal and fetal health; the risks of pharmacotherapy should be balanced against the risks of leaving the condition untreated. [[91]](/library/zO1rES0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>ECT</u> can be safely offered to pregnant and lactating patients who prefer to avoid pharmacotherapy. [[30]](/library/bWXHPC)




> [!WARNING]
> While <u>SSRIs</u> are generally compatible with <u>breastfeeding</u>, <u>infants</u> of <u>breastfeeding</u> mothers taking <u>SSRIs</u> should be monitored for signs of medication toxicity, such as excessive tiredness, irritability, and poor feeding. [[82]](/library/sO1tFS0)




#### Complications




Untreated <u>peripartum depression</u> can have adverse consequences.  [[82]](/library/sO1tFS0)[[91]](/library/zO1rES0)




* Maternal: <u>suicide</u>, impact on bonding

* <u>Newborn</u>: <u>infanticide</u>, <u>failure to thrive</u>, <u>developmental delay</u> [[96]](/library/vm1Ahh0)





#### Prevention




For patients at increased risk considering <u>pregnancy</u> :




* Consider <u>psychiatry</u> referral prior to <u>conception</u>.  [[91]](/library/zO1rES0)

* Recommend <u>psychotherapy</u>. [[84]](/library/wN1hWh0)





### Differential diagnosis of postpartum low mood
